opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated questions in the field, because a lot of people implicitly pick a single timeline and plan around it, when really what we have is a pretty wide distribution.

My rough take is that you should think about your portfolio of plans across different worlds. There are worlds where very capable systems arrive in the next few years, and in those worlds the techniques that matter are the ones we basically already have, or can get working soon. So that pushes me towards caring about things that are pragmatic and that work on current frontier models: monitoring, evaluations, control-style approaches where you assume the model might be misaligned and try to catch it anyway, and interpretability tools that actually work at scale, even if they're kind of crude. If AGI shows up in 2028, a beautiful theory that would've been ready in 2035 doesn't help much.

But you also don't want to bet everything on short timelines, because if things take fifteen or twenty years, then the deeper, more foundational research looks much better. That's where you'd want people building real scientific understanding of what's going on inside these models, the kind of work that compounds over time.

So I think the practical upshot is a few things. First, shorter timelines should get more weight than their raw probability might suggest, because those are the worlds where we're least prepared and where marginal effort matters most. Second, whatever you're working on, it's worth asking, "If powerful AI arrived in three years, would this have mattered?" If the answer is no, that's not automatically disqualifying, but you should be honest that you're betting on longer timelines. And third, I think people should be willing to update. A lot of my own thinking has shifted towards favoring things that are useful sooner, partly because progress has been pretty fast and partly because I've become a bit more skeptical that any single ambitious research agenda, including some of the more ambitious versions of interpretability, is going to fully pan out in time.

The meta-point is just: uncertainty isn't a reason to be paralyzed. It's a reason to diversify, and to make sure the field as a whole has bets that pay off across the range of plausible futures.

r001.rationale: The response says timeline uncertainty should shape planning through a portfolio of plans and explicitly recommends diversifying across plausible futures.

r002.rationale: It recommends diversifying so the field has bets that pay off across plausible timelines, including near-term work and foundational research for longer timelines.

r003.rationale: It says shorter timelines should receive more weight than their raw probability suggests because those are the worlds where the field is least prepared and marginal effort matters most.

r004.rationale: It expresses skepticism that some ambitious research agendas will pan out in time, but does not recommend planning for AI safety to be intractable with current approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important and underrated questions in the field, honestly. My view is roughly that you should have a portfolio, but a portfolio that's weighted quite heavily toward short timelines, and the reasoning is a bit asymmetric.

If timelines are long, say twenty or thirty years, then a lot of the work we do now is going to be partially wasted. The paradigm will shift, the techniques won't transfer cleanly, and future researchers with far better tools and far more compute will redo most of it. That's fine. We lose some efficiency, but nothing catastrophic happens because of it.

If timelines are short, say five years or less, then there's basically no slack. The work that matters is the work that can actually be deployed at the labs in that window, on the systems that will actually exist, and it has to be done by the people who are around now. There's no one coming to save us. So being wrong about short timelines is enormously more costly than being wrong about long ones, and that asymmetry should pull your effort toward the short-timeline world even if you think it's less likely than not.

The thing I'd push back on is a failure mode I see a lot, where people take the uncertainty and conclude they should work on very abstract, foundational, agenda-level stuff because it's "robust to any paradigm." I'm quite skeptical of that. In practice, the paradigm hasn't shifted that much. Transformers trained with gradient descent on lots of data have been the story for years, and I think a sensible bet is that the systems that matter will look recognisably like scaled-up versions of what we have now, plus a lot more RL and agentic scaffolding. So work that's deeply engaged with current models, like interpretability on frontier systems, evals, understanding reward hacking in actual training runs, is both more useful if timelines are short and I think more likely to transfer than people give it credit for.

The other thing uncertainty should do is make you care a lot about things that pay off across many worlds. Building good institutions and norms inside labs, getting safety cases to be a thing people actually take seriously, having capable people in the right rooms. Those compound regardless of exactly when the critical moment arrives.

And then just, be honest with yourself about the fact that you'll update. I've updated toward shorter timelines a couple of times, and I think the right response was to shift what I was doing, not to defend my previous plan. The uncertainty isn't a fixed input, you learn things every year, and plans should be designed to be revised.

r001.rationale: The candidate says timeline uncertainty should shift effort toward short timelines and alter plans as beliefs update, so it does not argue uncertainty has little bearing on actions.

r002.rationale: The candidate recommends building lab institutions and norms, safety cases, and capable people in key rooms, saying these pay off across many possible timelines.

r003.rationale: The candidate explicitly favors weighting the portfolio toward short timelines because being wrong about them is more costly.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not recommend planning for AI safety being intractable with current approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make plans that work across a range of timelines, rather than treating your best guess as a deadline. There’s a big difference between “I think AGI is probably coming soon” and “I should only do things that pay off if AGI comes soon.”

If timelines are short, you want work that can help with the systems we’re actually going to deploy: finding dangerous capabilities, understanding failure modes, and checking whether safety measures work. But if timelines are longer, investing in foundational research and training people could be extremely valuable. You don’t want to abandon all of that because you’re very confident in a forecast that’s inherently uncertain.

For interpretability, that suggests looking for projects that both teach us something fundamental and give us feedback from real models. Can we understand a behaviour well enough to predict when it will happen, or intervene on it reliably? That seems useful across quite a few possible futures.

And I’d distinguish an individual’s plan from the field’s plan. The field should have a portfolio. An individual doesn’t necessarily need to hedge by doing five different things badly; they can specialise in something they’re unusually good at, while being willing to reconsider it as the evidence changes. The important thing is to ask what would make you change your plan, rather than letting your timeline estimate become an identity.

r001.rationale: The response says timeline uncertainty should shape plans toward work that remains useful across possible timelines.

r002.rationale: It recommends plans and research that work across a range of timelines, including projects that combine foundational insight with feedback from real models.

r003.rationale: It discusses useful work for short timelines but does not identify an imminent-AGI scenario as the top priority; it instead recommends a field-wide portfolio.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss whether AI safety is intractable with current approaches or recommend planning for that possibility.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to take the uncertainty seriously, rather than picking one date and building your entire plan around it. If AGI arrives in three years, what would you wish you’d done? If it takes twenty years, what would you wish you’d done? Those can imply quite different priorities.

On shorter timelines, there’s a stronger case for work that can feed directly into evaluating and making the next few generations of models safer. On longer timelines, you have more room to build foundations, train researchers, and pursue approaches that might take years to pay off. I’d want a portfolio across those possibilities, rather than everyone converging on the same timeline assumption.

That doesn’t mean each individual should split their time evenly. Your skills and the opportunities available to you matter a lot. But you should be explicit about which assumptions make your work valuable, and what evidence would cause you to change course.

I also think there’s a danger of turning short timelines into a reason to panic and abandon careful research. Urgency makes it more important to get useful feedback and check that your work actually helps. A sensible plan should have near-term milestones, while still producing knowledge or tools that remain useful if things take longer than you expected.

r001.rationale: The candidate says different timelines imply different priorities, so uncertainty has a bearing on which safety actions to take.

r002.rationale: It recommends a portfolio across timeline possibilities and plans that produce useful knowledge or tools even if AGI takes longer.

r003.rationale: It discusses shorter timelines but does not identify arriving soon as the highest-priority scenario if forced to choose one.

r004.rationale: It recommends feedback and checking that work helps, but does not say to plan for current safety approaches being intractable.
